akhfash:5-5.t: He said ﴿فَجَعَلَهُمْ كَعَصْفٍ مَّأْكُولِ﴾. «[Translator's note: the source gives no comment after the quotation.]»

daas-irab:1-1.t: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾ the hamza is a particle of affirmative interrogation (istifhām taqrīrī), and an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by lam, the sign of its jussive being the omission of the weak letter from its end, and the fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir). ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ an interrogative noun, mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object). ﴿فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ﴾ a past verb and its fāʿil; the clause stands in place of the two objects of ترى. ﴿بِأَصْحابِ﴾ attached to (mutaʿalliq) the verb. ﴿الْفِيلِ﴾ muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct).

daas-irab:2-2.t: ﴿أَلَمْ يَجْعَلْ﴾ the hamza is a particle of affirmative interrogation (istifhām taqrīrī), and an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by lam, and the fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir). ﴿كَيْدَهُمْ﴾ mafʿūl bihi (direct object). ﴿فِي تَضْلِيلٍ﴾ attached to (mutaʿalliq) the verb; the clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa), with no grammatical position.

daas-irab:3-3.t: ﴿وَأَرْسَلَ﴾ a past verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir). ﴿عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ attached to (mutaʿalliq) the verb. ﴿طَيْراً﴾ mafʿūl bihi (direct object). ﴿أَبابِيلَ﴾ an adjective (ṣifa); the clause is conjoined (maʿṭūfa) to what precedes it.

daas-irab:4-4.t: ﴿تَرْمِيهِمْ﴾ an imperfect verb and its object, and the fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir). ﴿بِحِجارَةٍ﴾ attached to (mutaʿalliq) the verb. ﴿مِنْ سِجِّيلٍ﴾ an adjective (ṣifa) of حجارة; the clause is a second adjective of طيرا.

daas-irab:5-5.t: ﴿فَجَعَلَهُمْ﴾ a past verb and its object, and the fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir). ﴿كَعَصْفٍ﴾ attached to (mutaʿalliq) the verb, and the two are in the position of the second object. ﴿مَأْكُولٍ﴾ an adjective (ṣifa) of عصف; the clause is conjoined (maʿṭūfa) to what precedes it.

farraa:1-1.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَابِ ٱلْفِيلِ﴾.
He says: have you not been told about the Abyssinians? They had marched against the House and the people of Mecca. When they were at Dhū al-Majāz, they passed by a herdsman of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and drove off his camels. He mounted his riding animal and came to Mecca, cried out the cry of alarm, and then told them the news. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib leapt onto the back of his horse and caught up with them. Two men of Kinda and Ḥaḍramawt said to him: Go back [149/a] — they were friends of his. He said: By Allah, I will not leave until I take my camels or am taken with them. So they said to Aṣḥama, the chief of the Abyssinians: Give them back to him, for he will take them [back] in the morning [anyway]. So he returned with his camels and told the people of Mecca the news. They stayed for some days seeing nothing; then ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib went back to their place, and behold, they were as Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: "كالْعَصْف المَأْكُولِ" (like devoured straw). Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, had sent against them birds carrying in their beaks stones like sheep droppings; the bird would let go of the stone and it would not miss its man's head, and it would come out of his backside; so they killed them all. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib took of the yellow and the white — meaning gold and silver — as much as he wished, then returned to the people of Mecca and told them; and they went out to their camp and [plundered] what was in it. [Translator's note: the source has «فانتبهوا» (they became aware of), apparently for «فانتهبوا» (they plundered); translated by the latter.]

farraa:3-3.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿أَبَابِيلَ﴾.
It has no singular, like الشماطيط, العباديد and الشعارير [Translator's note: all words for scattered groups]; for none of these is a singular used. Al-Ruʾāsī — and he was trustworthy and reliable — claimed to me that he had heard its singular: إِبَّالة, with no yāʾ in it. And I have heard among the Arabs one who says: "ضِغث على إبَّالة" (a handful [of grass] on top of a bundle), meaning: plenty on top of plenty. As for «الإيبالة», it is the surplus of fodder that is on top of the load of a donkey or camel; it is like "plenty on plenty", and a load on top of a load. So if someone said: the singular of «الأبابيل» is إيبالة, it would be correct, as they said: دينار, دنانير. And one of the grammarians — al-Kisāʾī — said: I used to hear the grammarians say: أبوك, like العِجّول and العجاجيل. [Translator's note: «أبوك» is as printed; the parallel with «عجّول / عجاجيل» indicates the singular «إبّول».]

farraa:4-4.t: And it is said: ﴿سِجِّيلٍ﴾ is like baked brick, cooked from clay. Al-Kalbī said: Abū Ṣāliḥ narrated to me; he said: I saw in the house of Umm Hāniʾ bint Abī Ṭālib about a qafīz [Translator's note: a dry measure] of those stones, black and streaked with red.

farraa:5-5.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿كَعَصْفٍ﴾.
«العصف» is the tips of the crop before it ripens and forms ears.

zajjaj:1-1.t:
Sūrat al-Fīl
Meccan
﷽
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأصْحابِ الفِيلِ﴾ ("have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the people of the elephant?"): ”كَيْفَ“ is in the position of the accusative (fī mawḍiʿ naṣb) by ”فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ“, not by His saying ”ألَمْ تَرَ“, because ”كَيْفَ“ is one of the interrogative particles [and so is not governed by what precedes it]. The meaning of ”ألَمْ تَرَ“ is ”ألَمْ تَعْلَمْ؟“ ("have you not known?"). So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, informed His Messenger of narratives from the past and of what in them points to Allah's oneness and to His exalting the matter of His Kaʿba.
Part of the story of the people of the elephant is that a group of Arabs were in the land of the Negus, near a house that was a place of prayer for the Christians and the companions of the Negus. They kindled a fire which they used for some of their needs, then departed without putting it out; the wind carried it until it burned the house that was their place of prayer and a place of resort for the Negus and his companions. So he [Translator's note: the source does not name him; the account refers to the Abyssinian ruler's army, led in the usual narrative by Abraha] set out for Mecca, intending to burn the Sacred House and to make the people of Mecca lawful prey. When they drew near the Sanctuary (ḥaram), their mounts would not carry them toward the House, but when they turned them back they went. So Allah admonished them with the most eloquent of admonitions, yet they persisted in heading for the House and in [intending] to burn it. So Allah sent against them birds in flocks (abābīl), and made their plot go astray, that is, into loss and destruction. With each bird were three stones: a stone in its beak and two stones in its feet. A stone of them would fall on a man's head and come out of his rear; on each stone was the name of the man on whom it fell. So Allah, exalted be His praise, said: ﴿وَأرْسَلَ عَلَيْهِمْ طَيْرًا أبابِيلَ﴾ [al-Fīl: 3] ("and He sent against them birds in flocks"): groups from here and groups from there; and the meaning is: Allah sent against them these birds with these stones from every side.
And the meaning of ﴿تَرْمِيهِمْ بِحِجارَةٍ مِن سِجِّيلٍ﴾ [al-Fīl: 4] ("pelting them with stones of sijjīl"): Allah described, in the case of everyone He punished with stones, that they were ”مِن سِجِّيلٍ“; He said about the people of Lot: ﴿وَأمْطَرْنا عَلَيْها حِجارَةً مِن سِجِّيلٍ مَنضُودٍ﴾ [Hūd: 82] ("and We rained upon it stones of sijjīl, layered"). So the meaning is: "and He sent against them what pelted them with stones of sijjīl", that is, of His severe punishment. When the Arabs describe something hateful with sijjīl, they seem to mean severity by it, and nothing but what is hateful is described with it. The poet said:
وَرَجْلَةً يَضْرِبُونَ البَيْضَ ضاحِيَةً ∗∗∗ ضَرْبًا تَواصَتْ بِهِ الأبْطالُ سِجِّيلا
(And foot-soldiers striking the helmets in broad daylight, with a blow that heroes have commended to one another, severe [sijjīl].)
That is: a severe blow. As for ﴿أبابِيلَ﴾ [al-Fīl: 3], Abū ʿUbayda said: it has no singular. Others said: ”إبّالَةٌ“ and ”أبابِيلُ“; ”إبّالَةٌ“ being as if it were a group. Some said: its singular is ”إبُولٌ“ and [the plural] ”أبابِيلُ“, like ”عُجُولٌ“ and ”عَجاجِيلُ“.

zajjaj:5-5.t: ﴿فَجَعَلَهم كَعَصْفٍ مَأْكُولٍ﴾ ("and He made them like eaten-up straw"): that is, He made them like the leaves of crops that have dried and been eaten, that is, into which the eating blight (al-ukāl) has fallen. And it has come in the exegesis that Allah the Exalted sent a flood against them which carried them to the sea.
